Name: Roope Pöyry
aboutMeContent: Lead Developer with 9 years of experience across React, .NET, and Azure. I've built multiple services from scratch, modernized older systems, and enjoy the architecture and data modeling work that makes everything downstream easier. Recently focused on integrating AI-assisted development into both my own workflow and our team's processes.

content.EasyOpp:
At EasyOpp I lead architecture and engineering on the work-time platform — a connected system of payroll calculation and customer-configurable reporting that sits at the core of what the product does. Most of the work below was solo end-to-end, with scoping and spec collaboration where it mattered. Beyond what's listed, I also own the production deployment process, the Azure footprint, and the work-time automations pipeline. Two patterns recur across all of it: rehearsed migrations from dev through test to prod, and considered alternatives I rejected rather than just the one I shipped.

  • Configurable payroll calculation engine. Took over the calculation core from an outside consultant in early 2024 and redesigned it: shift-level aggregates became slot-level results so every payroll minute traces back to the time slot that produced it; two salary tables were consolidated into one; the user workflow collapsed from three button-pushes across two screens to one button on the same screen. Calculation correctness used to be one of our most common support-ticket categories; afterwards it dropped to rare edge cases plus extension requests for new functionality. The engine stays configurable enough that customers across multiple Finnish collective labor agreements all run on it with no per-agreement code paths — when a customer's agreement needs new rules, I extend the parameter set rather than branching the engine. Sole maintainer since.
  • Customer-configurable reporting platform. Designed and built the reporting system on top of the work-time data — a focused solo build in Q4 2025 on top of earlier groundwork. Pre-calculated from saved salaries (rather than on-demand) for performance and historical accuracy, with free-form JSON templates rather than a fixed schema, on the principle that customer customization can't be enumerated upfront. Report templates run in production today, some authored by customers themselves, some by the EasyOpp team for less technical ones.
  • Recurring shifts in the planning feature. Built the work-shift planning feature solo, with a recurring-shifts model that expands on demand: a stateless engine projects virtual shift instances at read time within the user's view window, rather than generating instance rows on a schedule. The choice was deliberate — a prior repeating-orders feature in the product had hit known limitations with the generation approach, and I wanted "every Tuesday forever" to be one row with zero instance rows by default. In production since launch with no critical issues and no dedicated owner — the design has been effectively maintenance-free, which is the outcome the model was chosen for.
  • Azure subscription migration with zero downtime. Planned and executed a full migration of the Azure footprint — compute, storage, networking, monitoring, and CI — to a new sponsored subscription. Cutover used parallel-run renamed App Services validated against real production data via local DNS overrides, then a DNS swap and traffic drain. Zero customer-visible downtime, ~12 months of free runtime on sponsored credits.
  • Claude Code adoption across the team. Introduced Claude Code end-to-end: project instructions, a GitHub Actions code-review pipeline, and custom skills — including a review-triage skill for collaborative interactive PR reviews. The workflow has matured through sustained tuning over the past few months. The design, integration, and ongoing tuning are mine.
content.Adalia:
Designing and developing web applications, both for customer projects across different industries and on our own Monitoring and Evaluation system.

Starting as a Junior Developer, my responsibilities grew over my time at Adalia — including mentoring new Junior Developers who joined after me. For some projects I was the sole developer responsible for maintenance, often handling multiple projects at the same time.

For one customer project I had the responsibility of starting the implementation of a completely new system from scratch: creating the application structure (React + Rails), designing the data model, and implementing user and permission management to provide a foundation for other developers to join the work.

In another project I implemented offline functionality, allowing data to be saved while the user is offline and synchronized to the server once the connection was available again. I also did my master's thesis on this specific subject, which included additional research on related topics like using service workers to cache application content in the browser.

The main technologies used were Ruby on Rails, React, and PostgreSQL. I also did configuration for services running on AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda, and worked on a Node.js API.
content.Other:
My side projects are small tools for my own family, in daily use rather than demos. They're also where I try out new stacks and AI-assisted ways of working before bringing them to the day job.

  • Family Planner. A weekly planner that reads the family's Google calendars and iCal feeds, applies our own planning rules, and shows ahead of time when there's real study time and how it divides between deadlines, warning early when an item won't fit. TypeScript end to end: a Hono API and a React PWA deployed as one Cloudflare Worker with D1, Google sign-in, and the planning rules in a pure, unit-tested package with no I/O. Playwright end-to-end tests run on desktop and phone viewports in CI. Each feature starts as a written spec, gets built in one Claude Code session and is tested against the spec in another. Started in late October 2026 and already in use.
  • Perheraha. A family finance app (Flutter, Riverpod, Drift / SQLite) that brings spending, net worth, subscriptions and accounts across several banks into one place, built around a low-friction monthly ritual instead of manual logging. Recent work added an MCP server, so Claude Desktop can run the monthly ritual against the app's database: importing statements, categorizing, finding refunds and updating balances, with a backup before every write. Alongside it came PSD2 bank sync, a Windows desktop build that syncs to the family's phones over home Wi-Fi, and refund and subscription price-change detection. Still no cloud backend: the data stays on our own devices.
  • Chore app. A Flutter app for kids who can't read yet: they tap a finished chore and earn collectible animals and vehicles that fill themed books and come alive in a tappable world with animations and sounds. Local-first SQLite, synced between the family's phones through Supabase. In use at home and updated regularly.
Earlier I also published Sleep Clock to the Play Store, a small utility I built as a React PWA.

content.Architecture:
Designing data models and overall system architecture is the part of the work I find most rewarding — getting the foundation right is what makes everything afterward easier or harder. Most of the architectural calls I make come down to thinking carefully upstream so the downstream work stays simple: choosing a data model that absorbs future variation rather than fighting it, picking deployment topology that matches how the work actually flows, and being deliberate about the seams between systems.

On cloud, I work primarily on Azure today (App Services, Azure Functions, Storage, SQL, SignalR, Bicep for everything) after earlier experience on AWS at Adalia (Fargate with load balancers, Lambda via Ruby on Jets API Gateway). The comparison has been useful — the platforms make different defaults feel natural, and seeing both makes it easier to recognize when you're fighting a default versus working with one.
content.AIAssisted:
Over the past year I've integrated Claude into both my own development workflow and our team's processes — using it for scoping work, prototyping features, and reviewing code more thoroughly. The shift has been bigger than I expected. It's changed how I approach problem decomposition, what kinds of refactors are worth tackling, and how quickly I can ramp on unfamiliar parts of a codebase.

It also changes the discriminator between engineers. The technical work itself gets faster, so the value moves further upstream — to clearly defining what to build, recognising when a generated solution is wrong in subtle ways, and making the architectural calls that AI tools can't make for you. Helping the team navigate that shift has become a real part of the Lead Developer role for me.

My side projects are where I work through these questions in practice, across whole small products. In Family Planner every feature runs through separate Claude Code sessions: one scopes it with me into a written spec, a fresh one implements it, and another tests it against the spec before it's deployed. In Perheraha I went the other direction and built an MCP server, so Claude Desktop can work on the app's own data, with guardrails like dry runs and a backup before every write. Both have taught me where AI shines and where it still needs careful human direction.
content.React:
I've worked with React from the start of my developer career — nine years now, in both TypeScript and JavaScript. Over that time I've designed and implemented several React applications from scratch, which has consistently been the best way for me to keep learning new things. I've also used React for personal projects, including this site and a small Android app I built as a React PWA and published to the Play Store.

I have experience with state management libraries like Redux and Redux Toolkit, and used Redux Offline for my master's thesis to provide offline functionality for users. I gravitate toward simple, reusable components and custom hooks that keep component logic clear and readable. The best thing about React is that there's always more to learn and improve on, even after this long with it.
content..NET:
I've worked with C# + .NET backends for over three years at EasyOpp. The production stack is currently .NET 8 with a .NET 10 upgrade landed and ready for rollout, and we use Entity Framework Core in our APIs with NUnit for unit tests. I've also worked with SignalR for sending real-time messages from the API to our React UI — automating much of what users would otherwise have to log manually.

Implementing the backend logic to create and update work-time entries based on vehicle location data, and then pushing those updates via SignalR, was one of the most interesting challenges I've worked on. The logic was complex with several configurable options, and the core has held up well — most of my recent work on it has been production hardening rather than new feature work, including a connection leak fix and batching changes that cut per-unit DB round-trips significantly. The transition from Rails to .NET went smoothly, and at this point I'm comfortable developing new features effectively while still picking up new things about the framework.
content.Flutter:
Flutter is the technology I've been deepening on the side, with two apps in daily use at home: Perheraha, a family finance app, and a chore app for young kids. Both use Riverpod for state management and Drift over SQLite for a local-first database.

What I've enjoyed most is how much of each app I've designed end to end on my own. In Perheraha that has meant working through more than ten schema migrations, CSV and PDF statement imports with duplicate detection, learned rules for category and subscription matching, and PSD2 bank sync. The same codebase also runs as a Windows desktop app that syncs to the family's phones over home Wi-Fi, and its database layer stays free of Flutter so a plain-Dart MCP server can share it. The chore app goes in a different direction: reward animations and a tappable world drawn with plain Flutter animations and CustomPainter, and sync between phones through Supabase with a trigger-filled outbox.

Mobile development has been a useful change of pace from web, and Flutter's one codebase for several platforms has proven itself in practice, not just in theory.
content.RubyOnRails:
I worked with Ruby on Rails for six years at Adalia, both maintaining existing systems and building completely new projects. I used Rails as a backend API for React frontends and as a more traditional MVC framework, set up unit tests with RSpec, and used the RSpec API Doc Generator to automate API documentation for one of the projects. I also implemented SAML authentication using Suomi.fi for a Rails + React project, allowing users to authenticate with their bank credentials.

Rails is a beginner-friendly and approachable framework, and while it's not where I'd start a new project today, I'd be happy to work with it again — there's a lot of well-earned wisdom baked into how the framework guides you toward sensible defaults.
